rv.q: McDonald’s “Rose’s Turn” feels like a once-in-a-lifetime event; the sort of unequivocal theater magic that you one day tell your grandkids about.
It is a once-in-a-lifetime performance (yours, not hers) that anyone would be crazy to miss.

However, the latest revival, shepherded by legendary director and playwright George C. Wolfe and starring Tony Award winner Audra McDonald, is an electric and truly unique production that will undoubtedly become a crowning jewel in the canon of “Gypsy.”
In "Gypsy," McDonald augments her unparalleled Broadway legacy by summoning America’s rueful history to the stage.
McDonald certainly makes a good a case as anyone ever has for Rose qualifying as a tragic hero, and more power to both her and her director.
In any case, no minor flaw can diminish the impact of this masterful show in such a beautifully acted production — all of it orbiting around the blazing force that is McDonald.
Any production of “Gypsy” rises or falls on its Rose, and Ms. McDonald’s lifts this staging to majestic (sorry) heights.
McDonald makes it sting, and makes this evergreen show business tragedy stick.
McDonald brings her formidable vocal gifts and dramatic intelligence to bear on one of the most demanding roles in the American musical theater canon, and the result is deeply satisfying.
McDonald's operatic soprano does much of that bridging work, connecting her Rose not to the bright trumpet hotcha of vaudeville but to the mad arias of Lucia di Lammermoor.
Woods is sensational, moving from heartbreaking vulnerability in 'Little Lamb' to slinky, Josephine Baker-esque confidence as she embraces her Gypsy Rose Lee striptease persona.
Wolfe’s Gypsy may flicker, but McDonald glows like a furnace at its center.
Better advice for next time would be: You gotta get a different director.
McDonald’s monumental performance and Wolfe’s intelligent staging make this an essential entry into the revival canon, and a production not to be missed.

McDonald’s Rose is the most tender version of the role that I can possibly imagine, and you can feel the love sparkle between her and her daughter Louise (a stunning Joy Woods, fresh of The Notebook) alongside the resentment.
Audra McDonald carries this revival on the strength of her performance, but this production wins hearts on its own for its tender portrayal of Broadway’s most iconic family.
McDonald's Rose is a force of nature, delivering a performance that is both deeply personal and universally resonant.

I can’t recall a better wrong-for-the-part performance in recent memory than McDonald’s Rose.
Gypsy remains magnificent, but this production—with its excellent singing and cast—requires a stronger conceptual execution to make it truly great.
Everything is indeed coming up roses for the best Gypsy and the best musical revival in years.
Luckily, McDonald offers the kind of fully committed, thoroughly thoughtful and often breathtaking performance people will talk about for decades.
McDonald's specificity and willingness to let Rose pull out all the stops and tumble into her own personal disarray is nothing less than miraculous.
All in all Gypsy impressed me on every level, and I am sincerely excited for potential nominations when awards season rolls around.

Those theatergoers who like their musical theater on the cutting edge will find this Gypsy invigorating.
Given the meatiest role of her storied career, Audra McDonald as Rose devours the stage while creating a monstrous but sympathetic character you will not forget.
By no means is this production terrible or unsatisfying, but it is not perfect.
